title: The Snow Day Fort
sum: On a snow day, Mia and Jonah build a snow fort block by block, fix dry snow, a melting wall and a missing roof, and finish with a cocoa party inside.

cast.d: a seven-year-old girl who loves plans and signs
cast.look: a seven-year-old girl with two brown braids, a red puffy coat and a striped knit hat with a pom-pom

cast.d: Mia's eight-year-old neighbor, full of ideas and songs
cast.look: an eight-year-old boy with curly black hair, a green snowsuit, one red mitten and one blue mitten

cast.d: Mia's dad, who knows about snow and owns the red sled
cast.look: a tall man with a short brown beard, a gray wool hat and a big snow shovel

cast.d: Mia's small dog, who wants to be in the fort all the time
cast.look: a small brown dog with floppy ears and a blue knit sweater
an older Korean woman with short gray hair, glasses and a long purple coat
a woman with curly black hair and a yellow knit scarf

p: Dad's phone buzzed at seven o'clock, and he grinned at the message. “No school today, Mia,” he said. “It's a snow day!”
Mia ran to the window. The yard was a big white pillow, and each fence post wore a tall white hat.
Jonah from next door was already outside in his green snowsuit. He had one red mitten and one blue one. “Mia!” he yelled. “Let's build a fort!”
Mia pulled on her boots so fast that she put them on the wrong feet. Her little dog, Waffles, ran out the door with her.
“A real fort,” Mia said. “With walls and a roof, and cocoa inside.” Waffles barked twice. That meant yes.
Dad brought an old blue bin from the garage. “First, pack the snow in hard,” he said. “Next, flip the bin over. Then tap the bottom. Last, lift.”
Mia packed, and Jonah flipped. Mia tapped, and Jonah lifted. Whoosh! The block fell apart, and Waffles sneezed in the powder.
Jonah tried to make a snowball instead. The snow ran out between his fingers like sugar. “This snow is broken,” he said.
Dad scooped some up and let it fall. “It's not broken. It's too cold and dry,” he said. “Dry sand won't make a sandcastle either.”
“So what do we do?” Mia asked. Dad pointed at the sky. “Wait for the sun. It will make the snow a little wet, and wet snow sticks.”
Waiting was the hardest part. They ate tomato soup, and Mia checked the window after every spoonful. By one o'clock, the sun was shining on the whole yard.
Mia squeezed some snow in her mitten, and it held its shape! Pack, flip, tap, lift. This time the block slid out whole, with flat sides and sharp corners.
“We did it!” Jonah threw both arms in the air. Waffles ran around the block three times.
Then they each made their own blocks. Mia made nine. Jonah only made seven, because every time he turned around, Waffles was sitting in his bin.
Two blocks went across the front, then a gap for the door, then two more. Three went down each side, and the rest started the next row.
When the sun slid down behind the trees, the wall only came up to Mia's knees. But Waffles walked right in and lay down, as if it were already his house.

art.s: Two children in snowsuits lift a blue plastic bin in a snowy backyard as the snow block falls apart and a small brown dog sneezes into the powder.

q.q: Why did the snow fall apart in the morning?
c: It was too cold and dry.
It was too wet and heavy.
q.e: Cold, dry snow is like dry sand. When the sun made it a little wet, it stuck together.

q.q: Draw Mia and Jonah when the first good block slid out whole. Show how they felt.
look: a snow block with flat sides and sharp corners
Jonah's arms up in the air
q.e: Hooray! Anyone can see how glad they were.

q.q: Mia made 9 blocks and Jonah made 7. How many blocks did they make in all?
q.e: 9 and 7 make 16. That was enough for the whole bottom row and a few more.

p: The roads were still icy the next morning, so school was closed again. Mia sat at the kitchen table and drew a plan for the snow fort.
The fence was the back wall. Across the front went two blocks, a door and two more blocks. With three blocks down each side, that made ten blocks in every row.
Jonah came in, stamping snow off his boots. “How many rows?” he asked. Mia chewed on her pencil. “Enough so we can sit inside and nobody can see us.”
Outside, Jonah sat in the snow by the wall, and Mia stacked blocks beside him. One, two, three, four. The fourth block reached the top of his hat.
“Four rows, with ten blocks in each,” said Mia. She started counting by tens on her fingers. Jonah flopped back in the snow. “That's a lot of blocks!”
Today the snow was sticky and perfect. Pack, flip, tap, lift. Jonah made up a song about it. Mia sang it too, but only in her head.
They set each new block over a crack, like bricks on a house. Row two went on, then row three.
Then Waffles bit a corner off a block and ran away with it. “That's a wall, not a snack!” Mia called after him.
By four o'clock, the last row was done. Mia crawled inside through the door and sat down. Only the pom-pom on her hat stuck up over the top.
Next came the sign. Jonah wrote the name on a piece of cardboard in big black letters: FORT FORSTY.
Mia giggled. “You mixed up the R and the O.” Jonah squinted at the sign. Then he crossed out the word and wrote FROSTY above it, with an arrow.
Under the name, Mia added a rule: FRIENDS AND DOGS ONLY. Waffles sniffed the sign and wagged his tail. He was allowed.
After dinner, Dad filled the watering can. “It will be very cold tonight,” he said. “Sprinkle the walls all over.” Mia and Jonah took turns until the can was empty.
In the morning, before the school bus came, Mia ran out to look. The walls were hard as rock. A thin shell of ice covered them, shiny like the glaze on a donut.
Jonah knocked on the wall. Knock, knock! Not one crumb of snow fell off. Mia hung the sign on the fence, crossed-out word and all.

art.s: A boy and a girl hang a cardboard sign that says FORT FROSTY, with a crossed-out word and an arrow, on a fence beside a shiny, ice-glazed snow-block fort.

q.q: The fort needed 4 rows, with 10 blocks in each row. How many blocks was that?
Mia and Jonah sprinkled water on the walls. What did the water turn into during the cold night?
q.e: The cold night froze the water into ice. That made the walls hard as rock.

q.q: Draw the sign for Fort Frosty. Write the name and the rule, then add one new rule of your own.
look: the rule FRIENDS AND DOGS ONLY
one new rule of your own
q.e: What a great sign! Now everyone knows the rules.

p: On Wednesday, school opened again, and the sun shone through the classroom windows all day. Mia kept drawing little forts on her math paper. Forty blocks, four rows of ten.
The bus dropped her off at half past three. Mia ran straight to the backyard, and Jonah ran out to meet her. Then they both stopped.
The front wall looked wrong. Its top was soft and shiny with water. Two blocks had slid down into a lumpy pile. Drip, drip, drip went the water into a puddle by the door.
“It's slouching,” said Jonah. He let his shoulders droop and his arms hang down, just like the wall. Mia laughed, even though her stomach felt heavy.
They counted the bad blocks. The top row of the front wall was mushy, and so were two blocks under it. That made six blocks to fix.
Then Mia looked at the side wall by the garage. It stood straight and hard, with sharp corners. She knocked on it, and it was hard as ice.
“Why did only one wall melt?” Jonah asked. Mia looked up. The garage made a long blue shadow over the side wall. But the front wall sat right out in the sun.
“The sun did it,” Mia said. “The shade kept the other wall cold.” Then she had an idea. “We need shade for the front, too!”
In the garage, behind the bikes, stood the red and white beach umbrella from summer. Jonah stared at it. “A beach umbrella? In winter?”
First, they fixed the wall. The snow was wet from the sun, so it packed well. Pack, flip, tap, lift. Six new blocks went back on top.
Then Jonah pushed the umbrella pole deep into the snow in front of the fort. Mia opened it wide, and its shadow fell right over the front wall.
Across the street, Mrs. Kim was shoveling her steps. She leaned on her shovel and called, “Going to the beach?” “Sort of!” Mia called back.
By dinnertime, the drip, drip, drip had stopped. Waffles lay in the striped shade with his eyes half closed. He looked like a dog on a beach vacation.

art.s: A red and white striped beach umbrella stands in the snow and shades the drooping front wall of a snow fort while a small brown dog naps under it.

q.q: Fort Frosty had 40 blocks. The sun melted 6 of them. How many good blocks were left?
q.e: 40 take away 6 is 34. Then they made 6 new blocks, and the fort had 40 again.

q.q: Jonah said the wall was “slouching.” What did he mean?
q.a: It was drooping down instead of standing up straight.
q.e: Slouching means not standing up straight. Jonah even slouched like the wall to show it!

q.q: Draw the fort in the afternoon sun. Show the wall in the sun and the wall in the garage's shadow.
look: the sun shining on the front wall
drips or a droopy top on the sunny wall
a straight, hard wall in the shadow
q.e: Great looking! The sun melted one wall, and the shade kept the other one cold.

p: On Saturday, the sky was gray and there was no sun at all. “Good fort weather,” said Dad. Fort Frosty stood hard and straight, but it still had no roof.
“A fort with no roof is just a box,” said Jonah. He patted snow into a long, flat slab and laid it across the top. It reached from one side wall to the other.
Crunch! The middle cracked, and the slab fell in. Waffles had been napping inside. He shot out the door like a furry white rocket, covered in snow.
“Sorry, Waffles!” Jonah brushed the snow off the dog's ears. Mia stared at the open top of the fort. “We need something long and flat that won't break.”
Then she remembered Dad's old red sled, hanging in the garage. It was long and flat, and it was made of hard plastic.
Would it be long enough? Mia walked her boots heel to toe across the gap between the side walls. It was five boots wide.
Then she walked her boots along the sled. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. “Seven boots!” Jonah said. “That's more than five!”
They lifted the sled together and set it on top. Each end rested on a wall. Then they piled snow on it and patted it flat, like a real white roof.
Mia ran inside and wrote on a sticky note. “Dear Dad, we borrowed your sled. It is a roof now. Love, Mia” She stuck it on the back door.
When they crawled in, it was dim and quiet, and the light looked a little blue. Outside, the wind blew snow off the fence in long white puffs. Inside, not one flake moved.
Mia pulled off one mitten, and her hand did not get cold. Waffles crept back in and squeezed between their knees. It was snug in there.
Soon Dad came out with the sticky note in his hand. He poked his head in the door. “So that's where my sled went.”
“It's warmer in here than out there,” Dad said. “Why is that?” Jonah listened to the wind go whoo-oo over the fence. “Because it can't get in,” he said.
Dad tried to crawl the rest of the way inside. His head and shoulders fit, but the rest of him did not. Waffles licked his nose.

art.s: Two children and a small brown dog sit snugly inside a snow fort with a red sled for a roof while a bearded dad pokes his head through the door holding a sticky note.

q.q: Why did Mia stick a note on the back door?
q.a: To tell Dad they borrowed his sled for the roof.
q.e: A note tells someone news when you can't tell them yourself. Now Dad knew where his sled went!

q.q: Why was it warmer inside the fort than outside?
c: The walls kept the wind out.
The sun came through the roof.
The sled made its own heat.
q.e: The cold wind blew outside, but it could not get in. Snow walls work like a thick coat.

q.q: The gap was 5 boots wide, and the sled was 7 boots long. Draw the sled roof on top of the fort.
look: a sled longer than the gap
both ends of the sled resting on the walls
q.e: Seven is more than five, so the sled reached all the way across!

p: On Sunday morning, Mia and Jonah made party invitations. Mia wrote each one in her best letters: “Come to Fort Frosty! Sunday at two o'clock. Bring mittens!”
Jonah drew a tiny fort on every card. They gave one to Dad, one to Jonah's mom and one to Mrs. Kim across the street.
At two o'clock, the guests came crunching across the yard. The grown-ups were too big for the door. So they sat outside on upside-down buckets, and Mia and Jonah sat inside.
Mrs. Kim bent down and peeked in at the icy walls and the sled roof. “My goodness,” she said. “It's magnificent, like a real castle.”
Dad carried out a tray with five cups of cocoa. Steam curled up from every cup into the cold air. He dropped three marshmallows into each one. Plop, plop, plop.
Waffles sat up very straight and stared at the marshmallows. He did not blink once. Jonah's mom laughed and gave him a dog biscuit instead.
Mia held her warm cup with both hands. Walls, a door, a roof and cocoa inside. It was the fort she had wanted since the very first snow day.
“Enjoy it,” Mrs. Kim said. “Spring always comes, and then the snow turns into water.” Mia looked at the icy walls. She did not want Fort Frosty to become a puddle.
Jonah sat up so fast that he bumped the roof. “Let's save some,” he said. “In the freezer!”
They each packed a round, hard snowball. Mia carried hers straight to the freezer. Jonah set his on the kitchen table while he pulled off his boots. Then he forgot all about it.
At dinnertime, Mia found a puddle on the table. Water dripped off the edge onto the floor, and Waffles licked it up. Jonah's snowball was gone.
Mia opened the freezer. Her snowball sat there, round and hard, with a little frost on top. The kitchen was warm, but the freezer was as cold as the backyard.
She put it in a plastic bag and wrote a label: FORT FROSTY. OPEN IN JULY. Then she tucked it behind the frozen peas.

art.s: Grown-ups sit on upside-down buckets outside a snow fort with a red sled roof, holding steaming cups of cocoa, while two children peek out of the door and a small dog stares at the marshmallows.

q.q: Mrs. Kim said the fort was “magnificent.” What did she mean?
q.e: Magnificent means grand and wonderful. She said it looked like a real castle!

q.q: Dad put 3 marshmallows in each of 5 cups. How many marshmallows was that?
Draw the two snowballs at dinnertime: Jonah's on the kitchen table and Mia's in the freezer.
look: a puddle of water on the table
a round, hard snowball in the freezer
something that shows warm or cold
q.e: Nice thinking! The warm kitchen melted the snow into water, and the cold freezer kept it frozen.

fin.q: On the first day, Mia and Jonah made 16 blocks. The finished walls had 40 blocks. How many more blocks did they make after the first day?
fin.e: Count up from 16: 4 more makes 20, and 20 more makes 40. That is 24 more blocks.

fin.q: The cold night, the umbrella's shade and the freezer all helped the snow. What did they do?
fin.e: Snow stays snow when it stays cold. Warmth turns it into water.
